about: The Catena Aurea's quotations left out, and notes on who some of its names are. The founder's decisions of 2026-10-21 (docs/FOUNDER-DECISIONS.md, the shortlist's answer 5 and decision 23, items 2 and 9): hide Origen, Didymus and the Arian writer of the unfinished work on Matthew with a visible line where each stood; hide Clement of Alexandria's one quotation; keep Eusebius with a note; keep Victor of Antioch in Mark; label Josephus a witness. Each rule's count is what it finds in the pinned copy, and the build fails if that changes. Sources were read on 2026-11-22; their words are in docs/voices/checks/catena-aurea.md.

hide.name: Pseudo-Chrysostom
hide.chapters_why: The unfinished work on Matthew has no homilies on chapters 26 to 28; the quotations there are from sermons once credited to Chrysostom (Hom. de Cruce, Hom. in Pass., Hom. de Resur.) and stay.

origen.why: The anathemas of the Second Council of Constantinople, in 553, name Origen and his writings.

src.label: the council's eleventh anathema
quote: If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches and Origen, as well as their impious writings...

didymus.why: Didymus wrote a work defending the teaching of Origen's First Principles.

src.label: the Catholic Encyclopedia, Origen and Origenism
quote: Didymus the Blind composed a work to explain and justify the teaching of the "De principiis"

clement.why: The Gelasian Decree lists Clement of Alexandria's works among the books the Church does not receive.

src.label: the Gelasian Decree
quote: The remaining writings which have been compiled or been recognised by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church does not in any way receive
LIKEWISE A LIST OF APOCRYPHAL BOOKS
the works of the other Clement, of Alexandria | apocrypha

arian-matthew.why: The unfinished work on Matthew was once thought to be Chrysostom's; it was written by a follower of Arius in the first half of the 400s.

src.label: the Catholic Encyclopedia, St. John Chrysostom
quote: The most important spurious work in Latin is the "Opus imperfectum", written by an Arian in the first half of the fifth century

who.name: Eusebius
who.note: bishop of Caesarea and church historian (born about 260, died before 341), whom Arius named on his side before the Council of Nicaea; he then signed its creed

src.label: the Catholic Encyclopedia, Eusebius of Caesarea; Theodoret, Church History 1.4; Socrates, Church History 1.8
quote: Eusebius Pamphili, Bishop of Cæsarea in Palestine, the "Father of Church History"; b. about 260; d. before 341.

https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/27021.htm, Arius to Eusebius of Nicomedia: "Eusebius, your brother bishop of Cæsarea, Theodotus, Paulinus, Athanasius, Gregorius, Aetius, and all the bishops of the East, have been condemned..."
https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/26011.htm, Socrates on Eusebius at Nicaea: "at length acquiesced in it, and subscribed it with all the rest."

who.name: Josephus
who.note: the Jewish historian of the first century, quoted by Aquinas as a witness; not a Christian writer

src.label: Smith's Bible Dictionary, the entry on Matthew, in the copy the app ships (smith_bibledict.xml)
quote: The Jewish historian Josephus furnishes an illustration of the fate of the Hebrew original of Matthew.
Josephus himself informs us that he, wrote his great work "The History of the Jewish Wars," originally in Hebrew
